<p class="eyebrow">Research questions, contributions, and methods</p>
<p class="lede">My research concerns credit-risk model updating under distribution shift and diagnostic methods for extreme losses. I examine how limited data affect model selection, predictive accuracy, and the reliability of tail-risk estimates.</p>

<p class="meta">Research manuscripts are identified by their current working status. No publication or journal acceptance is implied. <a href="https://orcid.org/0009-0002-5110-8102">ORCID profile</a> · <a href="https://github.com/sdbambil1">GitHub</a></p>

## Tail Model Diagnostics Using Expected Shortfall and Bounded Loss Layers with an Application to Fire Losses {#fire-loss}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil, Shudeshna Nandy, Clement Ampong, Prakash Karki, and Chi-Kuang Yeh</p>

High-loss quantiles can agree even when expected tail losses differ. This study evaluates fitted tail models using Expected Shortfall and bounded loss layers, with an application to U.S. structure-fire losses.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

The study uses established stop-loss identities to relate aggregate Expected Shortfall discrepancies to expected losses within bounded layers. It develops diagnostic comparisons and inferential procedures that account for empirical averaging and model estimation using the same observations. Simulations assess detection, localization, and uncertainty separately; identifying a discrepancy does not by itself determine where it occurs.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and application</summary>

The study uses Peaks-Over-Threshold and Generalized Pareto modeling, bounded-layer expectations, simulation, and uncertainty assessment. Its empirical application considers structure-fire losses recorded in the 2016–2025 U.S. National Fire Incident Reporting System releases. Particular attention is given to sparse extreme observations and the influence of exceptionally large incidents.

</details>

## Selection Regret in Credit-Risk Model Updating Under Distribution Shift: The Role of Recent Labeled Information {#selection-regret}

This study asks whether selecting the oracle updating policy more frequently necessarily reduces the predictive cost of selection mistakes. It examines how the amount of recent labeled information affects decisions to retain, recalibrate, or refit a credit-risk model.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

The study distinguishes the probability of choosing the best fitted candidate from the regret associated with choosing another candidate. Across 13 simulated scenarios, mean selection regret was lower with 10,000 recent labeled observations than with 2,500, but oracle agreement did not improve uniformly. Under stability, oracle agreement fell from 27.6% to 23.6% as mean selection regret fell by approximately 76.7%. Selection frequency alone is therefore an incomplete measure of decision quality.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and evidence</summary>

Simulation experiments compare model-updating choices under different shift conditions and adaptation-sample sizes. Stratified cross-validation is used for policy selection, and independent evaluation data are used to measure predictive loss. A historical mortgage-data application provides an additional comparison. Results are interpreted in terms of fitted-candidate regret rather than an unattainable population oracle.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Credit risk</span><span>Selection regret</span><span>Validation</span><span>Distribution shift</span></div>

## Selecting and Estimating Credit-Risk Model Updates Under Distribution Shift {#distribution-shift}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil and Shudeshna Nandy</p>

Updating a credit-risk model requires a choice between retaining the existing model, recalibrating its predictions, and refitting its coefficients. This study examines the trade-off between allocating labeled observations to selecting an updating procedure and using those observations to estimate the updated model.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

Using mortgage-anchored simulations and historical cohorts, the study compares validation-guided selection with unrestricted and regularized refitting under a common labeled-data budget. Validation-guided selection can outperform unrestricted full-budget refitting when adaptation data are scarce, but it does not uniformly outperform regularized full-budget estimation. The results underscore the separate roles of intervention selection, model estimation, and label allocation.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and methods</summary>

The study uses historical mortgage cohorts and controlled simulations under covariate, baseline-risk, and predictor-effect shifts. It compares retention, recalibration, unrestricted and regularized refitting, validation allocation, and post-selection refitting, with independent assessment of predictive performance.

</details>
